justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I'd assume is a current level near 495–500 on the S&P 500 (or a similar broad equity index). At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 498.5 essentially anchors near the prevailing price with only a slight drift, since daily returns are dominated by noise rather than any directional signal. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 501, reflecting the historically positive drift in equity markets while acknowledging that a single week still offers very little room for that drift to accumulate meaningfully. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 508 incorporates a more visible expected return — roughly 1–2% above the starting point — consistent with long-run average monthly equity returns, absent any strong near-term macro signal pulling me strongly in either direction.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially across horizons, and this is driven primarily by the compounding of daily volatility over time. At one day, typical realized volatility in equity markets translates to a fairly tight range. Over a week, that uncertainty expands by roughly the square root of five, and over a month it widens further still. The wide one-month interval of 450 to 566 reflects not just statistical volatility scaling but also the possibility that within a month, a meaningful macro development — such as a central bank surprise, an inflation print, or a geopolitical shock — could shift the regime entirely. I also weighted the intervals slightly asymmetrically to account for the well-documented tendency of equity selloffs to be sharper and faster than rallies.

The most meaningful tail risks that could push outcomes beyond my stated intervals include a sudden, large interest rate move driven by an unexpected inflation or employment report, a geopolitical escalation that triggers risk-off flows, or a significant earnings disappointment from a large-cap company that cascades into broader sentiment deterioration. On the upside, a dovish pivot signal from a major central bank or a strong economic data surprise could fuel a sharp rally. Liquidity conditions also matter — in thinner trading environments, moves can overshoot fundamentals considerably.

It is worth being transparent that these forecasts carry substantial epistemic uncertainty beyond just market volatility. I do not have access to real-time price data or current news, so my starting level and recent trend assumptions are themselves uncertain. If the actual current price differs meaningfully from my assumed anchor, all three estimates would shift accordingly, and the intervals should be understood as centered on whatever the true current level is rather than on any precise number I've stated.
